newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Upper house rejects Waigel's tax reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Upper house rejects Waigel's tax reform.

text.p: Germany's opposition-controlled upper house of parliament, or Bundesrat, on Friday rejected -- as expected -- Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax reforms for 1998 and 1999.
The two bills now go to parliament's mediation committee.

They passed comfortably in the lower house, or Bundestag, last week with the votes of deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democratic Union (CDU), Christian Social Union (CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP).

But the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who hold a majority in the Bundesrat, have criticised Waigel's plans to cut taxes by a net 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) over the next two years as socially unjust and fiscally unsound.

The SPD said the bills would rip open a 45 billion mark ($26 billion) financing gap in federal, state and local budgets, provide little relief for low-wage earners and would not boost investment because they did not lower wage costs.
The legislation now passes to the mediation committee where next Thursday 16 representatives from both the Bundestag and the Bundesrat will try to thrash out a compromise.

"We are prepared to reach an agreement," said Henning Voscherau, Hamburg mayor and SPD negotiator in tax talks with Chancellor Kohl's coalition. "But not at any price. I will not hold out my hand for the ruination of my budget."
The tax reform, which was amended in committee, would cut the lowest rate of income tax to 15 percent in 1999 from 39 percent, while the top rate would fall to 39 percent from 53 percent.

The solidarity income tax surcharge, raised to help rebuild ex-communist eastern Germany, would fall to 5.5 percent from 7.5 percent next year. The top rate of corporation tax would fall in two steps to 35 percent by 1999 from 45 percent now.

The Federation of German Industry has called the tax reform a scandal, saying changes to corporate taxes would effectively raise taxes on industry by 13.7 billion marks next year and only offer promise of relief in 1999.
The German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) called the rejection of the bills a "disappointment".
"If nothing is decided in German economic and tax policies this autumn German industry will lose two to three decisive years in international competition," it said.
"These are years in which our competitors on global markets will expand their market share."
Waigel defended the tax cuts and urged the SPD to end its reform blockade in the interest of jobs and economic growth.
"The mere agreement on a comprehensive, workable (tax) concept would stimulate the economy," he said.
"Economic fundamentals are in order, interest rates are low, prices are stable. Why, then, is unemployment rising in spite of economic recovery?"
Waigel said structural problems were strangling the economy and these could only be addressed by broad fiscal reform.
But Voscherau said that while German companies complained of high taxation, many of the country's blue-chip firms took advantage of loopholes and paid relatively little or no tax.
"Whoever achieves record corporate profits and pays 20 to 30 percent in taxes and then badmouths the Fatherland because of high tax rates is a liar and is just poisoning the well," said Voscherau.
Hermann Otto Solms, parliamentary leader for the FDP in the Bundestag, said the rejection of the tax reform was thoughtless and would waste time needed to get the economy back on track.
"In the face of 4.6 million unemployed we need a signal for more investment and more jobs now and not to wait until kingdom come," he said.
-- William.Boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 490 228 26097 150)
